title: Test Harness: Who Has This Number?
subtitle: Three providers and Ofcom answer “who has this number?” for an unported and a ported number, running live in your browser.
endNote: Point your own code at the live test provider: pstn2.org/testcp

segments.text: This is the PSTN2 test harness. Everything on screen is running live in your browser, using the same discovery engine our software development kits are tested against.
At the top is Ofcom. Its numbering list shows each block of numbers, the provider it is allocated to, and the new PSTN2 field: the Range Holder’s web address.
Below are three providers: Alpha Telecom, Bravo Networks and Charlie Comms. Each one is the Range Holder for one block.
Each provider keeps its own number database: the range Ofcom allocated to it, the numbers it has in service, the numbers ported in, and, as Range Holder, where its ported-out numbers went.
Notice the ported numbers. 0113 496 0456 started with Charlie, and now lives with Bravo. And 020 7946 0321 moved from Alpha to Charlie.
There is no central database anywhere on this screen.

scenes.title: Every provider keeps a copy of Ofcom’s list

segments.text: Before any calls, each provider downloads Ofcom’s numbering list and keeps a local copy. That happens about once a day, never once per call.
Each provider also has a cache, empty for now, where it will remember the answers it receives.
First call. An Alpha Telecom customer dials 0161 496 0123.
Alpha checks its cache. Nothing there yet.
So it searches its copy of the numbering list. The block 0161 496 0 belongs to Bravo Networks, and the list gives Bravo’s address.
segments.say: So it searches its copy of the numbering list. The block oh one six one, four nine six, oh, belongs to Bravo Networks, and the list gives Bravo’s address.

segments.text: Alpha asks Bravo: who has 0161 496 0123? Bravo checks its own database. The number is in service, and it has never moved.
Bravo answers: held. Alpha caches the answer. One query, and the call can be routed.
Second call. The same customer dials 0113 496 0456.
Another cache miss. The numbering list says this block belongs to Charlie Comms, so Alpha asks Charlie.
Charlie is the Range Holder, and its database shows the number was ported out to Bravo. So Charlie answers with a redirect, including Bravo’s address.
Alpha follows the redirect and asks Bravo. Bravo’s database shows the number as ported in from Charlie, so Bravo answers: held.
Alpha caches the answer against that one number. Two queries, and the answer is authoritative.

scenes.title: Scenario C · The next call goes direct

segments.text: A few minutes later, someone else at Alpha calls 0113 496 0456.
This time the cache has the answer. Alpha skips the numbering list and the Range Holder, and asks Bravo directly.
Bravo confirms: held. One query. This is what most calls look like once a network has warmed up.

scenes.title: Scenario D · The number moves again

segments.text: Now the customer ports again, from Bravo back to Charlie. Watch the databases.
Bravo removes its ported-in record, and Charlie, the Range Holder, marks the number as back in service. Nobody tells Alpha, and nobody needs to.
Alpha’s next call relies on its cache, so it asks Bravo. Bravo no longer holds the number, and answers: not held. Invalidate your cache.
Alpha deletes the cached entry and starts again from the numbering list. The Range Holder is Charlie, and Charlie now answers: held.
The stale entry cost one extra query, not a failed call. The cache has corrected itself.

scenes.title: When there is no PSTN2 answer

segments.text: Two more cases complete the picture.
Alpha dials 0161 496 0999. Bravo is the Range Holder, but the number is not in service, so Bravo replies: not found. The call is handled exactly as it is today.
Then 0117 496 0555. The numbering list shows Delta Voice, which has not published a PSTN2 address.
Delta has not joined yet, so the call simply uses today’s network. Participation is optional.
Now it is your turn. Choose the calling provider, pick or type a number, and press Discover.
You can also port a number to a different provider, and watch the caches correct themselves on the next call. Press Reset to start again.
Every message is real. These are the same requests and answers our software development kits exchange with the live test provider at pstn2.org.
